name: Adoni-bezek
summary: Judah defeated the Canaanite king Adoni-bezek and cut off his thumbs and great toes. He said it himself: seventy kings with thumbs and toes cut off had gathered their meat under my table; as I have done, so God hath requited me.
offense: Judah went up first at the Lord's word, with Simeon his brother, and the Lord delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they slew ten thousand men in Bezek (Judges 1:1-4). The king who fled from that field had made a practice of mutilation and counted it as his glory. He says the number himself: threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table (Judges 1:7). Seventy kings maimed so that they could neither hold a sword nor stand in a rank, kept alive to eat scraps as a display of his power. The law of Israel limits punishment to measure, breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again (Leviticus 24:19-20); he had exceeded all measure seventy times.
judgment: They pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes (Judges 1:6): the same mutilation, once. The verdict is pronounced by the condemned man himself, and the record leaves it in his mouth: as I have done, so God hath requited me (Judges 1:7). A Canaanite king recognised the measure of the God of Israel from his own case and named it as justice. They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died (Judges 1:7). Christ states the rule he fell under as a rule for everyone: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again (Matthew 7:2).

verses.text: And they found Adoni–bezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
But Adoni–bezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.

And Adoni–bezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.
And if a man cause a blemish in his neighbour; as he hath done, so shall it be done to him;
Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth: as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again.
And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life,
Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
Burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.

lawDetails.text: The restitution and punishment should be according to the crime--Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
If a man causes injury or blemish to another, he shall have the same injury done to him.
Punishment is the fruit and reward for iniquity and wicked ways (you shall reap that which you sow).

entries.commentary: After the death of Joshua the children of Israel ask the Most High who shall go up first against the Canaanites, and the answer is Judah: behold, I have delivered the land into his hand. Judah asks Simeon his brother to come up with him into his lot, and promises to go likewise with Simeon into his lot, so Simeon went with him.

The Most High delivers the Canaanites and the Perizzites into Judah's hand, and they slay ten thousand men in Bezek. Adonibezek flees and is caught, and his thumbs and great toes are cut off. He confesses it himself: threescore and ten kings with their thumbs and great toes cut off gathered their meat under his table, and as he had done, so God requited him.

The children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, smote it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire. This verse ties back into the history we just finished reading in Joshua. Judah was supposed to drive the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of the land, but could not, and the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Judah at Jerusalem. Jerusalem sat right on Judah's border by the valley of the son of Hinnom. The king of Jerusalem was already among the kings of the land which the children of Israel smote and whose land they possessed, so this fight in Judges is Judah taking the city itself.

Judah goes down against the Canaanites in the mountain, the south, and the valley, and against Hebron, which before was called Kirjath-arba, slaying Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. Caleb offers Achsah his daughter to wife to whoever smites Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, takes it. Achsah asks her father for a blessing, springs of water with the south land, and Caleb gives her the upper springs and the nether springs. This is a review of the history we just read in Joshua; it was not that many days ago in the reading that we covered this, and it repeats again here at the opening of Judges.

The children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, go up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah and dwell among the people in the wilderness of Judah. Judah goes with Simeon his brother, slays the Canaanites in Zephath and utterly destroys it, calling the city Hormah, and takes Gaza, Askelon, and Ekron with their coasts. The Most High was with Judah, and he drave out the inhabitants of the mountain, but could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.

Hebron is given unto Caleb, as Moses said, and he expels thence the three sons of Anak. The children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem, but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day.

The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel, which before was called Luz, and the Most High was with them. The spies see a man come out of the city and promise him mercy for showing the entrance. They smite the city with the edge of the sword, but let the man and all his family go, and he goes into the land of the Hittites and builds a city and calls it Luz.

Tribe after tribe repeats the same failure: neither did Manasseh, nor Ephraim, nor Zebulun, nor Asher, nor Naphtali drive out the inhabitants of their cities, and the Amorites forced the children of Dan into the mountain. What we are reading is how we did not drive out all the inhabitants of the land, which the Most High had commanded us. Each tribe did not drive them out, and what did we do? We dwelt among them. When Israel was strong, we put the Canaanites to tribute, but we still did not utterly drive them out; we still dwelt among them. Chapter 2 gets into what that dwelling among the inhabitants of the land brought upon us.

The children of Israel were commanded to bring pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamps to burn continually. Aaron ordered it from the evening unto the morning before the Lord continually, upon the pure candlestick, a statute for ever in your generations.

Twelve cakes of fine flour were set in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the Lord, with pure frankincense upon each row, every sabbath, taken from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant. It shall be Aaron's and his sons', and they shall eat it in the holy place, for it is most holy unto him of the offerings of the Lord made by fire.

The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the children of Israel, and strove in the camp with a man of Israel, and blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed. His mother was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan. They put him in ward, that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them; and the Lord commanded that he that had cursed be brought forth without the camp, that all that heard him lay their hands upon his head, and that all the congregation stone him. The strife in the camp likely arose from a man of Israel correcting him concerning the law. His father being an Egyptian shows he was conceived while Israel was in captivity in the land of Egypt, dwelling among the Egyptians; in the same way Moses, outside of Egypt with Jethro the priest of Midian, took a wife there. And there is no such thing as being half Israelite or a fourth Israelite: if your parent is Israel, you are Israel. Whosoever curseth his God shall bear his sin, and he that blasphemeth the name of the Lord, he shall surely be put to death, as well the stranger as he that is born in the land.

He that killeth any man shall surely be put to death, and he that killeth a beast shall make it good, beast for beast. If a man cause a blemish in his neighbour, as he hath done, so shall it be done to him: breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. One manner of law stood for the stranger as for one of your own country. When Christ came he taught the proper understanding of eye for eye for dealing inside the nation: ye have heard that it hath been said, an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth, but I say unto you that ye resist not evil. As the Son of God he had authority to magnify the law: whosoever smites thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; if any man sue thee and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also; whosoever compels thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Inside our nation we must practice forgiveness, patience, and long-suffering; we are dealing with our own people, brothers with a conscience. We are the most forgiving people on the planet; the only time we do not know how to forgive is when it comes to each other, and Christ dealt with that.

If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him. Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment for a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman sold unto thee. [Nehemiah 5](/bible/nehemiah/5) shows how brethren came into servitude: in the dearth some mortgaged lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn, some borrowed money for the king's tribute, and some brought their sons and daughters into bondage. The brother that waxes poor is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, and not ruled over harshly. If the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master's, and he goes out by himself; he did not bring them in. His two choices are to go out alone, or to plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever. Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

If a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do. The reason is that her master betrothed her to himself, or unto his son; she is a wife, not a six-year servant, so the release of the menservants does not apply to her. If she please not her master who hath betrothed her to himself, he must let her be redeemed; he has no power to sell her unto a strange nation, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her. The deceit is that he betrothed her to himself and then would not deal with her, keeping her to himself when she could have been another man's wife. If he take him another wife, her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage shall he not diminish; the duty of marriage is the marriage bed. If he lay with her, she belongs to him and he cannot send her away; and if he do not these three unto her, then shall she go out free without money. He must take care of her.

If a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand, a place was appointed whither he shall flee. That is the case of the slayer that kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when a man hews wood with his neighbour and the axe head slips from the helve and lights upon him that he die: he flees to the appointed city and lives, lest the avenger of blood overtake him while his heart is hot, for he was not worthy of death, having hated him not in time past. But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there.

If men strive and one smite another so that he keep his bed, he that smote him shall pay for the loss of his time and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. That is restitution: paying for the time the man was down and could not work and provide for his family. That is what the court system calls a civil suit today.

If a man smite his servant with a rod and he die under his hand, he shall surely be punished; but if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his money. The wisdom writings teach not to be ashamed of much correction of children, nor of making the side of an evil servant to bleed. An evil servant that will not get right could be corrected physically, so long as he was not killed.

If men strive and hurt a woman with child so that her fruit depart from her, this judgment covers the miscarriage: if no mischief follow, he is punished as the woman's husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and if any mischief follow, then life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound.

If an ox gore a man or a woman that they die, the ox is stoned and his flesh not eaten, and the owner is quit. But if the ox were wont to push with his horns in time past, and it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in, and it kill a man or a woman, the ox is stoned and his owner also put to death. Most do not have oxen today, but the same judgment reaches the yard dogs, the pit bulls, German shepherds, and rottweilers. If the dog has bitten before and it was reported to you, and it gets out again through a snapped chain or a breach in the fence and mauls or kills somebody, the scripture holds the owner responsible unto death; that is why animal control writes the ticket and warns you to keep your dogs in. The law is slack right now, as Habakkuk says, so many punishments worthy of death in the scriptures, like rape or this judgment, come out today as a fine or a slap on the hand.
